questions.subject: androl
questions.title: Upper limit for abnormal sperm forms
questions.question: The abnormal forms of sperms should not exceed ......... of the total count:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 2% is far below the accepted upper limit; a semen sample this clean of abnormal forms is unremarkable, not a threshold value.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 5% likewise sits well under the accepted ceiling for abnormal sperm morphology.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 10% is still below the conventional cut-off used in this bank.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 15% is closer to the true figure but is not the value this bank's key marks.
explanations.E: Correct. A normal semen sample may contain a substantial minority of morphologically abnormal sperm — forms with head, neck or tail defects — without this being considered pathological, and the accepted upper limit taught here is 20% of the total count. Once the proportion of abnormal forms rises above this figure (teratospermia), fertilising capacity is considered impaired even if the sperm count and motility are otherwise normal. This is one of the four classic semen-parameter thresholds tested alongside sperm count, motility and viability.

questions.learning_objective: State that abnormal sperm forms should not exceed 20% of the total count.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8, row-position 1 (unlabeled top row, e/20%.)
field_notes.reuse: Overlaid onto the live CON-AND-09727CBEB501FB (general infertility-association fact) rather than minted fresh — same semen-morphology idea, this question supplies the specific numeric threshold the live definition does not state.

questions.subject: androl
questions.title: Sperm viability after ejaculation
questions.question: Sperms remain viable after ejaculation for about:

explanations.A: Correct. Once ejaculated into the female genital tract, sperm remain capable of fertilising an ovum for approximately 2 days, after which their motility and fertilising capacity decline sharply even though some may still be present. This is the figure used clinically to define the fertile window together with the ovum's own much shorter post-ovulatory lifespan (about 24 hours) — together they give roughly a 3-4 day fertile window per cycle when sperm survival is counted backwards from ovulation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 3 days overstates the sperm's practical fertilising window as taught in this bank, though isolated sperm have occasionally been recovered later.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 4 days is well beyond the accepted viability window.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 5 days is well beyond the accepted viability window.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 6 days is well beyond the accepted viability window.

questions.learning_objective: State that ejaculated sperm remain viable for about 2 days.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 1 (a/2 days)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Cell type released at ovulation
questions.question: At time of ovulation, the ovary liberates:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A "mature ovum" only exists after the second meiotic division completes, which happens at fertilisation, not at ovulation — the popular term "egg" is loose shorthand for what is actually still a secondary oocyte at the moment it is released.
explanations.B: Correct. Ovulation releases a secondary oocyte, arrested in metaphase of the second meiotic division, surrounded by its zona pellucida and corona radiata. It only completes meiosis II — becoming a true mature ovum and extruding the second polar body — if a sperm penetrates it; if fertilisation never occurs, the secondary oocyte degenerates still arrested at metaphase II.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The second polar body is a discarded product of the second meiotic division, released only at fertilisation, not at ovulation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The primary oocyte is the cell present before the first meiotic division completes; that division finishes just before ovulation, converting the primary oocyte into the secondary oocyte that is actually released.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The oogonium is the diploid stem cell of oogenesis, present only in fetal life long before ovulation ever occurs.

questions.learning_objective: State that the ovary releases a secondary oocyte, not a mature ovum, at ovulation.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 2 (b/at ovulation the ovary releases 2ry oocyte)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Cell with 23 chromosomes
questions.question: Which of these cells contains 23 chromosomes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A daughter spermatogonium is a mitotic product of a stem-line spermatogonium and, like all pre-meiotic germ cells, is still diploid with 46 chromosomes.
explanations.B: Correct. The secondary spermatocyte is the product of the first meiotic division, so it carries the haploid number of 23 chromosomes — 22 autosomes and either an X or a Y. This halving happens well before spermiogenesis remodels the resulting spermatid into a mature sperm. The primary spermatocyte that produced it, by contrast, was still diploid with 46 chromosomes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The primary spermatocyte exists before the first meiotic division completes and so is still diploid, with 46 chromosomes arranged as duplicated (tetrad) chromatids.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The oogonium is the diploid stem cell of the female germ line, with 46 chromosomes, present only in fetal life.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A daughter oogonium is a mitotic product of an oogonium and remains diploid with 46 chromosomes.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the secondary spermatocyte as the first cell in the male germ line to carry 23 chromosomes.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 3 (b/2ry spermatocyte)
field_notes.reuse: Overlaid onto the live Kasr concept CON-DEV-0BA870DF2C2E13 ("each gamete nucleus carries 22 autosomes and one sex chromosome"), the broad haploid-formula record this and several later items in this cluster all draw on, rather than minting a narrow per-cell duplicate.

questions.subject: gyn
questions.title: Duration of progesterone secretion by the corpus luteum of pregnancy
questions.question: Corpus luteum of pregnancy continues to secrete progesterone for:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 9 days is well short of the corpus luteum of pregnancy's active lifespan; it describes roughly the time from ovulation to the point implantation is complete, not the corpus luteum's own endocrine lifespan.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 15 days is close to the lifespan of the corpus luteum of menstruation (which regresses after about 12-14 days if fertilisation fails), not the corpus luteum of pregnancy, which is rescued and persists far longer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 20 days is still well short of the corpus luteum of pregnancy's true active period.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 2-3 months undershoots the figure this bank's key marks, though it is in the right general range.
explanations.E: Correct. Once implantation rescues the corpus luteum from regression, human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) from the syncytiotrophoblast keeps it secreting progesterone for roughly 3-4 months (to about the end of the first trimester). After that point the placenta itself has taken over as the dominant source of progesterone, and the corpus luteum of pregnancy is no longer clinically necessary to maintain the pregnancy — this handover is why removing the corpus luteum in the first trimester can cause miscarriage but doing so later usually does not.

questions.learning_objective: State that the corpus luteum of pregnancy secretes progesterone for about 3-4 months before the placenta takes over.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 4 (e/corpus luteum of pregnancy remains up to 4 months)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Diploid cell among sperm-line cells
questions.question: Has diploid number of chromosomes:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A mature sperm is the final haploid product of spermatogenesis, carrying only 23 chromosomes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The secondary oocyte is haploid, carrying 23 chromosomes, since it forms only after the first meiotic division completes.
explanations.C: Correct. The primary spermatocyte is produced by mitotic growth of a spermatogonium and exists before the first meiotic division reduces the chromosome number, so it is still diploid, with 46 chromosomes present as duplicated chromatids. It is the last diploid cell in the male germ line — the secondary spermatocyte that results from its division is already haploid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An immature sperm (spermatid) is already haploid, the product of the second meiotic division.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The spermatid is haploid, formed by the second meiotic division of the secondary spermatocyte; it only remodels (spermiogenesis), it does not divide again.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the primary spermatocyte as the last diploid cell in the male germ line.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 5 (c/1ry spermatocyte)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Diploid cell among oocyte-line cells
questions.question: Which of the following cells is diploid:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The mature sperm is haploid, the final product of spermatogenesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The secondary spermatocyte is already haploid, the product of the first meiotic division of the primary spermatocyte.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The spermatid is haploid, the product of the second meiotic division.
explanations.D: Correct. The primary oocyte is arrested in prophase of the first meiotic division from before birth until just before ovulation, so throughout this long arrest it remains diploid, with 46 chromosomes present as duplicated chromatids. It is the female germ line's counterpart to the primary spermatocyte — the last diploid cell before meiosis reduces the chromosome number.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The second polar body is a haploid discard product of the second meiotic division, released at fertilisation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the primary oocyte as the last diploid cell in the female germ line.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 6 (d/1ry oocyte)

questions.subject: androl
questions.title: Meaning of necrospermia
questions.question: The term necrospermia in an ejaculate means:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Absence of sperm in the ejaculate is azoospermia, not necrospermia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A low sperm count is oligospermia, not necrospermia.
explanations.C: Correct. Necrospermia describes an ejaculate in which the spermatozoa present are dead (non-viable). This distinguishes it from asthenospermia (sperm that are alive but poorly motile) and from azoospermia (no sperm present at all). The sperm count itself can be entirely normal in necrospermia, since the defect is in viability, not in numbers.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Abnormally shaped sperm describes teratospermia, not necrospermia.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A high sperm count has no specific name relevant to this terminology set and is not necrospermia.

questions.learning_objective: State that necrospermia means the sperm present in the ejaculate are dead.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 7 (c/necrospermia=dead sperms)

questions.subject: obs
questions.title: Source of the hormone maintaining the corpus luteum during pregnancy
questions.question: The hormone that maintains the corpus luteum during pregnancy is produced by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The anterior pituitary drives the ovarian cycle before conception (via FSH and LH), but it is not the source of the hormone that rescues the corpus luteum once pregnancy begins.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ovary is where the corpus luteum itself is located and secretes progesterone, but the rescuing signal that keeps it active comes from outside the ovary.
explanations.C: Correct. The chorion — specifically its syncytiotrophoblast layer — secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) beginning soon after implantation. hCG has LH-like activity and rescues the corpus luteum from its usual 12-14 day regression, keeping it secreting progesterone and maintaining the endometrium until the placenta itself takes over steroid production later in the first trimester.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The epiblast contributes to the embryo proper and the amniotic cavity lining, not to hCG production.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The hypoblast contributes to the yolk sac lining, not to hCG production.

questions.learning_objective: State that the chorion produces the hCG that maintains the corpus luteum of pregnancy.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 rows 8-9 (c/chorion secretes chorionic gonadotropins which maintain corpus luteum of pregnancy)
field_notes.reuse: Overlaid onto the live CON-OBS-24CAE6B0880C64 ("Placental hCG maintains corpus luteum and promotes endometrial growth") rather than minted fresh — same fact; field_notes there already used "placental" loosely for the chorion/trophoblast source this question names specifically.

questions.subject: androl
questions.title: Organelle of origin of the sperm acrosome
questions.question: The acrosome of sperm is derived from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mitochondria migrate to and coil around the proximal part of the sperm tail to form the middle-piece sheath; they play no role in forming the acrosome.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The chromatin network condenses within the nucleus during spermiogenesis; it is not the source of the acrosome, which is a separate cytoplasmic structure covering the nucleus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The centriole forms the axial filament (axoneme) of the sperm tail, not the acrosome.
explanations.D: Correct. During spermiogenesis, proacrosomal granules accumulate within the Golgi apparatus of the spermatid and fuse into a single acrosomal vesicle, which then spreads over the anterior half (leading edge) of the condensing nucleus to form the acrosomal cap. This cap contains the hydrolytic enzymes (acrosin, hyaluronidase) released during the acrosome reaction that let the sperm penetrate the corona radiata and zona pellucida.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum is not the organelle of origin for the acrosome; that role belongs to the Golgi apparatus.

questions.learning_objective: State that the sperm acrosome is derived from the Golgi apparatus.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 10 (d/golgi apparatus)
field_notes.reuse: Overlaid onto the live CON-AND-4B7E5925250531 ("Acrosomal vesicle spreads over the anterior half of the nucleus to form an acrosomal cap") — same fact, this question and Q11 both test it from slightly different angles (organelle name vs part-of-spermatid framing).

questions.subject: androl
questions.title: Part of the spermatid that forms the acrosome
questions.question: The acrosome of sperm is derived from which part of the spermatid?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The nucleus condenses separately during spermiogenesis; the acrosomal cap forms over it but does not arise from it.
explanations.B: Correct. Proacrosomal granules accumulate within the Golgi complex of the spermatid and coalesce into the acrosomal vesicle, which spreads over the anterior half of the condensing nucleus as the acrosomal cap. This is the same fact tested from the organelle-name angle elsewhere in this set: the Golgi apparatus and the Golgi complex are the same structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mitochondria form the middle-piece sheath of the sperm tail, not the acrosome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The centriole forms the axial filament of the tail, not the acrosome.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Most of the spermatid's residual cytoplasm is shed during spermiogenesis, not incorporated into the acrosome.

questions.learning_objective: State that the acrosome forms from the Golgi complex of the spermatid.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 11 (b/golgi complex)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Timing of the oocyte's first meiotic division
questions.question: The oocyte completes its first meiotic division just before:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fertilisation is when the second meiotic division completes, not the first.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Gastrulation happens in week 3, long after both meiotic divisions of the oocyte have completed or been triggered.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Implantation happens about a week after fertilisation, well after the first meiotic division is complete.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Puberty marks when the arrested primary oocytes resume meiosis cycle by cycle, not when any single oocyte completes its first division.
explanations.E: Correct. The primary oocyte is arrested in prophase of the first meiotic division from before birth. Each cycle, a dominant follicle's oocyte resumes and completes this first division only shortly before ovulation, producing the secondary oocyte (and the first polar body) that is then released. The second meiotic division, by contrast, remains arrested at metaphase and completes only if fertilisation occurs — the two divisions are timed at opposite ends of the fertile window.

questions.learning_objective: State that the oocyte's first meiotic division completes just before ovulation.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 12 (e/1st meiotic division is completed just before ovulation); stem re-read by render (p.3) after OCR scrambled option order

questions.subject: androl
questions.title: Largest spermatogenic cell
questions.question: The largest spermatogenic cell is the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The oogonium belongs to the female germ line, not the spermatogenic series, so it is not a candidate answer here.
explanations.B: Correct. The primary spermatocyte is the largest cell in the spermatogenic series: it results from the growth phase of the spermatogonium (during which the cell enlarges considerably while its DNA replicates) and then persists through the long first meiotic prophase, growing further before it finally divides. Every cell downstream of it — the secondary spermatocyte, spermatid and sperm — is progressively smaller as division and remodelling proceed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The secondary spermatocyte is smaller than the primary spermatocyte that produced it, and short-lived besides, since it proceeds almost immediately to the second meiotic division.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The spermatid is considerably smaller, having already halved its chromosome content twice by the time it forms.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The mature sperm is the smallest and most compact cell in the series, having shed most of its cytoplasm during spermiogenesis.

questions.learning_objective: State that the primary spermatocyte is the largest cell in the spermatogenic series.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 13 (b/1ry spermatocyte); stem re-read by render (p.3) after OCR mangled it into unreadable fragments

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Phase of oocyte arrest until puberty
questions.question: In what phase does the oocyte become arrested until puberty?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Metaphase of meiosis II is the second, shorter arrest point the secondary oocyte reaches — at ovulation, not from fetal life to puberty — and it lasts only until fertilisation, not until puberty.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Meiosis II prophase is not a recognised arrest point for the oocyte at any stage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Metaphase of meiosis I is not where the long fetal-to-puberty arrest occurs; the oocyte is arrested earlier, in prophase.
explanations.D: Correct. All primary oocytes complete DNA replication and enter the first meiotic prophase during fetal life, then become arrested at the diplotene stage of that prophase. This arrest lasts from before birth until puberty, when — cycle by cycle, for whichever follicle becomes dominant — the arrest is finally released and the first meiotic division completes.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Option D correctly names the arrest point, so "none of the above" is not correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that the primary oocyte is arrested in prophase of the first meiotic division from fetal life until puberty.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 14 (d/arrested prophase of meiosis I); stem re-read by render (p.3)

questions.subject: gyn
questions.title: Cells surrounding the released secondary oocyte
questions.question: After ovulation, the released secondary oocyte is surrounded by cells called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The fimbriae are finger-like projections of the fallopian tube's infundibulum that sweep the released oocyte into the tube; they are not cells surrounding the oocyte itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The zona pellucida is a non-cellular glycoprotein layer immediately around the oocyte's own membrane, not the layer of cells asked for here.
explanations.C: Correct. The cumulus oophorus is the cluster of granulosa cells that remains attached to and surrounds the oocyte when it is expelled at ovulation. Its innermost, most tightly adherent layer is specifically called the corona radiata; together these follicular cells travel with the oocyte into the fallopian tube.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Acrosomes are a structure of the sperm head, unrelated to the cells surrounding an ovulated oocyte.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Oogonia are diploid stem cells present only in fetal ovarian tissue, not cells found around an ovulated oocyte.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the cumulus oophorus as the cell layer surrounding the ovulated secondary oocyte.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 15 (c/cummulus oophorus); stem re-read by render (p.3)
field_notes.reuse: Overlaid onto the live CON-GYN-67FBF69E18FC33 rather than minted fresh.

questions.subject: androl
questions.title: Meaning of azoospermia
questions.question: Complete absence of sperms in the semen is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Teratospermia describes an excess of abnormally shaped sperm, not absence of sperm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Necrospermia describes dead sperm present in the ejaculate, not their complete absence.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Oligospermia describes a low sperm count, which still means some sperm are present, unlike complete absence.
explanations.D: Correct. Azoospermia (spelled "azospermia" in this bank) is the complete absence of sperm in the ejaculate, distinguishing it from oligospermia (a low but non-zero count). It may be obstructive (sperm are produced but blocked from reaching the ejaculate) or non-obstructive (a primary failure of spermatogenesis itself).
explanations.E: Incorrect. Hypospermia describes an abnormally low semen volume, a separate parameter from sperm presence or count.

questions.learning_objective: State that azoospermia means complete absence of sperm in the semen.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 16 (d/azospermia=absent sperms); stem re-read by render (p.3)
field_notes.reuse: Overlaid onto the live CON-AND-614CCD51AB977A rather than minted fresh.

questions.subject: androl
questions.title: Spermatogenesis phase without division
questions.question: Which of the following phases of spermatogenesis shows no division?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Proliferation (mitotic multiplication of spermatogonia) and growth (enlargement into the primary spermatocyte) both precede division, but growth itself is paired here with proliferation, which does involve division, making this pairing wrong for a "no division" answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Proliferation is a mitotic, dividing phase, so pairing it with maturation does not describe a division-free stage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Maturation is the meiotic phase (primary spermatocyte to secondary spermatocyte to spermatid) and is full of division; pairing it with growth does not describe a division-free stage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This repeats option B; proliferation is a dividing phase, so it cannot be part of a "no division" pairing.
explanations.E: Correct. Spermatogenesis is conventionally divided into proliferation (mitotic multiplication of spermatogonia), growth (enlargement into the primary spermatocyte), maturation (the two meiotic divisions), and transformation (spermiogenesis, the remodelling of the spermatid into a sperm). Growth and transformation are the two stages that involve no cell division at all — growth is pure cellular enlargement, and transformation is a remodelling of an already-formed haploid spermatid, not a further division of it.

questions.learning_objective: Identify growth and transformation as the two phases of spermatogenesis that involve no cell division.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 17 (e/growth & transformation show no division); stem re-read by render (p.3), option D is a printed repeat of option B in the original scan

questions.author_notes: Options B and D are printed identically ("Proliferation & maturation") in the source scan, confirmed by direct render, not an OCR artefact -- kept verbatim as a genuine (if unusual) duplicate distractor rather than silently altering one.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Normal diploid chromosome number in the human somatic cell
questions.question: The normal diploid chromosome number in the human somatic cell is:

options.A: 46 autosomes + 2 sex chromosomes (which must be identical)
options.B: 46 autosomes + 2 sex chromosomes (which may be same or different)
options.C: 44 autosomes + 2 sex chromosomes (which must be identical)
options.D: 44 autosomes + 2 sex chromosomes (which may be same or different)

explanations.A: Incorrect. The total of 46 chromosomes is right, but they are not split as "46 autosomes plus 2 sex chromosomes" — the 46 already includes the 2 sex chromosomes, leaving only 44 autosomes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Same error as option A: describing 46 autosomes on top of 2 sex chromosomes overcounts the total to 48.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The autosome count of 44 is right, but the sex chromosomes are not required to be identical — only a female's are (XX); a male's are different (XY).
explanations.D: Correct. A normal human somatic cell is diploid with 46 chromosomes in total: 22 homologous pairs of autosomes (44 chromosomes) plus one pair of sex chromosomes. That sex-chromosome pair may be identical (XX, female) or different (XY, male), which is exactly why the correct description must allow for either.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 45 autosomes plus 1 sex chromosome describes a haploid gamete's autosome count with an odd total, not the diploid somatic cell this question asks about, and it also miscounts the autosome pairs (22 pairs = 44, not 45).

questions.learning_objective: State that the normal human somatic cell has 44 autosomes plus 2 sex chromosomes, which may be the same or different.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 18 (d/human somatic cell contains 44 autosomes + 2 sex chromosomes, same or different); stem re-read by render (p.4)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Chromosomal pattern of the oogonium
questions.question: Match each cell with its corresponding chromosomal pattern. Oogonium:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 45X (a single X with no autosome count stated) is the Turner-syndrome karyotype shorthand, not a normal germ-cell pattern.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 22X or 22Y is the haploid formula of a secondary spermatocyte or sperm, not the diploid oogonium.
explanations.C: Correct. The oogonium is the diploid stem cell of the female germ line, present only before birth. Like every diploid cell it carries 46 chromosomes in total. In the female these are arranged as 44 autosomes plus two X chromosomes (44XX).
explanations.D: Incorrect. 22X is the haploid formula of the secondary oocyte or ovum, not the diploid oogonium.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 44XY is the diploid male pattern, appropriate to the primary spermatocyte, not the female oogonium.

questions.learning_objective: Match the oogonium to the diploid 44XX chromosomal pattern.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 19 (c); matching set, stem+options read by render (p.4)
field_notes.asu: Embryo1 p.4 Q19, matching item 1 of 5 (Q19-23).

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Chromosomal pattern of the primary spermatocyte
questions.question: Match each cell with its corresponding chromosomal pattern. Primary spermatocyte:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 45X is the Turner-syndrome karyotype shorthand, not a normal germ-cell pattern.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 22X or 22Y is the haploid formula reached only after the primary spermatocyte divides; the primary spermatocyte itself is still diploid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 44XX is the diploid female pattern, appropriate to the oogonium, not the male primary spermatocyte.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 22X is a haploid formula, and specifically the female one; the primary spermatocyte is diploid and male.
explanations.E: Correct. The primary spermatocyte is produced by growth of a spermatogonium and exists before the first meiotic division reduces the chromosome number. It therefore retains the full diploid complement of 46 chromosomes. In the male these are arranged as 44 autosomes plus one X and one Y chromosome (44XY).

questions.learning_objective: Match the primary spermatocyte to the diploid 44XY chromosomal pattern.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 20 (e); matching set, stem+options read by render (p.4)
field_notes.asu: Embryo1 p.4 Q20, matching item 2 of 5.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Chromosomal pattern of the secondary spermatocyte
questions.question: Match each cell with its corresponding chromosomal pattern. Secondary spermatocyte:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 45X is the Turner-syndrome karyotype shorthand, not a normal germ-cell pattern.
explanations.B: Correct. The secondary spermatocyte is the haploid product of the first meiotic division of the primary spermatocyte. Because the primary spermatocyte carries one X and one Y chromosome, that division segregates them apart, so any given secondary spermatocyte ends up with 22 autosomes plus either an X or a Y — never both.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 44XX is a diploid female pattern, not the haploid secondary spermatocyte.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 22X alone (without the "or 22Y" alternative) is the female haploid pattern of the secondary oocyte, not the male secondary spermatocyte, which can carry either sex chromosome.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 44XY is the diploid pattern of the primary spermatocyte, one stage earlier than the haploid secondary spermatocyte this question asks about.

questions.learning_objective: Match the secondary spermatocyte to the haploid 22X-or-22Y chromosomal pattern.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 21 (b); matching set, stem+options read by render (p.4)
field_notes.asu: Embryo1 p.4 Q21, matching item 3 of 5.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Chromosomal pattern of the secondary oocyte
questions.question: Match each cell with its corresponding chromosomal pattern. Secondary oocyte:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 45X is the Turner-syndrome karyotype shorthand, not a normal germ-cell pattern.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 22X or 22Y is the male haploid pattern (secondary spermatocyte or sperm), since only the male carries a Y chromosome to segregate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 44XX is a diploid female pattern, not the haploid secondary oocyte.
explanations.D: Correct. The secondary oocyte forms when the first meiotic division of the primary oocyte completes, just before ovulation. Since the oogonium's diploid pattern was 44 autosomes plus two X chromosomes, the haploid secondary oocyte carries 22 autosomes plus a single X chromosome — there is no Y to segregate to, unlike the male line.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 44XY is the diploid male pattern, not applicable to the female secondary oocyte.

questions.learning_objective: Match the secondary oocyte to the haploid 22X chromosomal pattern.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 22 (d); matching set, stem+options read by render (p.4)
field_notes.asu: Embryo1 p.4 Q22, matching item 4 of 5.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Chromosomal pattern of the sperm
questions.question: Match each cell with its corresponding chromosomal pattern. Sperm:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 45X is the Turner-syndrome karyotype shorthand, not a normal germ-cell pattern.
explanations.B: Correct. The sperm is the final haploid product of spermatogenesis, unchanged in chromosomal content from the secondary spermatocyte that produced it (spermiogenesis remodels the cell's shape but is not itself a division). It therefore carries 22 autosomes plus either an X or a Y chromosome, and it is this X-or-Y that determines the offspring's sex at fertilisation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 44XX is a diploid female pattern, not the haploid sperm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 22X alone, without the "or 22Y" alternative, is the female haploid pattern (secondary oocyte), not the sperm, which may carry either sex chromosome.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 44XY is a diploid male pattern (the primary spermatocyte), not the haploid mature sperm this question asks about.

questions.learning_objective: Match the sperm to the haploid 22X-or-22Y chromosomal pattern.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 23 (b); matching set, stem+options read by render (p.4)
field_notes.asu: Embryo1 p.4 Q23, matching item 5 of 5.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Chromosomal formula of the first polar body
questions.question: The chromosomal formula of the 1st polar body is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 22+Y is not a possible formula for any oocyte-line product, since the oocyte carries only X chromosomes, never a Y.
explanations.B: Correct. The first polar body is the small, largely cytoplasm-free discard produced when the primary oocyte completes its first meiotic division. Since that division is a reduction division of a 44XX diploid cell, the first polar body — like the secondary oocyte it is expelled alongside — carries the haploid formula of 22 autosomes plus one X chromosome (22+X).
explanations.C: Incorrect. 44+XY is a diploid male formula and is not possible for any product of oogenesis, which never carries a Y chromosome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 44+XX is the diploid formula of the primary oocyte itself, before the first meiotic division; the first polar body is a haploid product of that division, not the diploid cell that produced it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Option B correctly gives the formula, so "none of the above" is not correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that the first polar body carries the haploid formula of 22 autosomes plus one X chromosome.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 24 (b/1st polar body=22+X)

questions.subject: androl
questions.title: Duration of spermatogenesis
questions.question: The time required for a spermatogonium to become a mature sperm is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Two days is far too short; spermatogenesis is a multi-week process.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ten days is far too short for the full sequence of proliferation, growth, the two meiotic divisions and spermiogenesis.
explanations.C: Correct. The complete transformation of a spermatogonium into a mature spermatozoon, passing through proliferation, growth into a primary spermatocyte, the two meiotic (maturation) divisions, and spermiogenesis, takes approximately 60-64 days in humans. Sperm then require a further period of epididymal transit and maturation before they are fully motile and fertile, which is counted separately from this spermatogenic timeline.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 50 days undershoots the accepted duration.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 73-75 days overshoots the accepted duration for spermatogenesis itself, though it is closer to figures sometimes quoted once epididymal transit time is included.

questions.learning_objective: State that spermatogenesis takes about 60-64 days.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 25 (c/60-64 days)

questions.subject: androl
questions.title: Cell that does not undergo cell division
questions.question: Which of the following cells does not undergo a cell division?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The primary spermatocyte does divide — it undergoes the first meiotic division, producing two secondary spermatocytes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The secondary spermatocyte does divide — it undergoes the second meiotic division, producing two spermatids.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The primary oocyte does divide — its first meiotic division, though long delayed, still completes just before ovulation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The secondary oocyte does divide — it completes its second meiotic division at fertilisation (if fertilisation occurs).
explanations.E: Correct. The spermatid is already the haploid end-product of the second meiotic division. It does not divide again; instead it undergoes spermiogenesis, a purely structural remodelling (acrosome formation, nuclear condensation, tail formation, shedding of cytoplasm) that converts it into a mature sperm without any further reduction or multiplication of its chromosome content.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the spermatid as the germ cell that does not undergo a further cell division.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 26 (e/spermatids undergo spermiogenesis with no cell division)

questions.subject: androl
questions.title: Spermiogenesis events, EXCEPT
questions.question: Spermiogenesis includes all the following EXCEPT:

options.D: Formation of a mitochondrial helical sheath

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this is a true event of spermiogenesis, not the exception). Proacrosomal granules from the Golgi apparatus do coalesce to form the acrosomal cap.
explanations.B: Correct -- this is the false statement, the exception. Golgi material forms the acrosomal cap over the nucleus, not the tail. The tail's axial filament (axoneme) instead arises from the centriole, and its surrounding mitochondrial sheath comes from mitochondria migrating to the middle piece -- the Golgi apparatus contributes nothing to the tail at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this is a true event, not the exception). The nucleus does condense markedly during spermiogenesis, becoming small, dense and hyperchromatic to fit the streamlined sperm head.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this is a true event, not the exception). Mitochondria do migrate to and wrap helically around the proximal tail to form the mitochondrial sheath of the middle piece.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. this is a true event, not the exception). Most of the spermatid's cytoplasm is indeed shed as the residual body during spermiogenesis, leaving the compact, streamlined mature sperm.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that Golgi material forms the acrosomal cap, not the sperm tail, as the false statement about spermiogenesis.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 27 (b/golgi material forms the acrosomal cap)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: What the sperm must undergo before fertilisation
questions.question: Before fertilization, the sperm must undergo:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Completing the second meiotic division is what the oocyte, not the sperm, does at fertilisation -- the sperm itself is already a fully haploid cell long before this point.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Spermiogenesis is the structural remodelling of the spermatid into a mature sperm, completed in the testis well before ejaculation, not a step required immediately before fertilisation.
explanations.C: Correct. In the female genital tract, the sperm must undergo capacitation: the removal of the glycoprotein coat and seminal plasma proteins from the membrane overlying the acrosome. Only a capacitated sperm can bind the zona pellucida's receptors and undergo the acrosome reaction, which is the immediate prerequisite for penetrating the corona radiata and zona pellucida to reach and fuse with the oocyte membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The acrosome is already formed during spermiogenesis in the testis, long before fertilisation; what happens near fertilisation is the acrosome reaction (release of the acrosome's contents), not its formation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The sperm's tail is lost after it enters the oocyte cytoplasm, not as a step required before fertilisation can occur.

questions.learning_objective: State that the sperm must undergo capacitation before it can fertilise an oocyte.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.8 row 28, letter column confirmed "c" by a second zoomed crop of the same cell (image characters distinguishable from "d"); the remark text on that row reads "Acrosome formation" verbatim, matching option D's wording rather than option C's -- treated as a source transcription slip, see author_notes

questions.author_notes: The printed key's letter (c) and its own remark text ("Acrosome formation", which is option D's wording, not option C's "Capacitation") conflict on this one row -- confirmed by a zoomed re-crop of the table cell that the printed letter really is "c", not a misread "d". Followed the letter, since (1) capacitation, not acrosome formation, is the standard immediate-prerequisite fact this stem is built to test -- acrosome formation happens in the testis during spermiogenesis, well before fertilisation, so "before fertilization the sperm must undergo acrosome formation" would be a poorly-formed question, while capacitation is exactly and only a pre-fertilisation event; and (2) the remark column has one clear, confirmed transcription error elsewhere in this same table (a wrapped two-line remark that visually displaced a row-number by one, resolved separately in the seed header) showing the remarks column is the less reliable of the two on this scan. Flagged for a human answer-key check rather than silently resolved with full confidence.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Chromosomal formula of the normal secondary oocyte
questions.question: The chromosomal formula of the normal human 2ry oocyte is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 44 autosomes + 2 X chromosomes is the diploid oogonium's formula, not the haploid secondary oocyte's.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 45 autosomes is not a valid haploid autosome count (22 pairs halve to 22, not to a number that would pair with a leftover 45).
explanations.C: Incorrect. A Y chromosome is never present in an oocyte-line cell; only sperm can carry a Y.
explanations.D: Correct. The secondary oocyte forms when the primary oocyte (44 autosomes + 2 X chromosomes) completes its first meiotic division, halving the chromosome number. It therefore carries the haploid formula of 22 autosomes plus a single X chromosome, exactly matching the secondary spermatocyte or sperm's autosome count but always with an X rather than a possible Y.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Two X chromosomes with only 22 autosomes mismatches a true haploid reduction; halving 44+2X gives 22 autosomes plus one X, not two.

questions.learning_objective: State that the secondary oocyte carries 22 autosomes plus one X chromosome.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 29 (d/2ry oocyte=22 autosomes+1 X chromosome); stem+options read by render (p.5)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Non-cellular layer secreted around the ovum
questions.question: The non-cellular layer that is secreted around the ovum is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The corona radiata is cellular -- a layer of follicular (granulosa) cells, not a non-cellular secretion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cumulus oophorus is likewise cellular, the broader mass of granulosa cells surrounding the oocyte.
explanations.C: Correct. The zona pellucida is an acellular glycoprotein coat, secreted by the growing oocyte itself (and, in part, its surrounding granulosa cells) directly around the oocyte membrane. It carries the species-specific sperm-binding receptors that a capacitated, acrosome-reacted sperm must engage to fertilise the oocyte, and it later blocks polyspermy once the first sperm fuses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The theca folliculi is a cellular layer of the ovarian follicle wall, external to the granulosa cells, not a non-cellular layer around the ovum itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The stratum granulosum is the cellular granulosa-cell layer lining the follicle, not a non-cellular secretion around the ovum.

questions.learning_objective: State that the zona pellucida is the non-cellular layer secreted around the ovum.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 30 (c/zona pellucida is non-cellular); stem+options read by render (p.5)
field_notes.reuse: Overlaid onto the pending Alexandria concept CON-DEV-642BA9E28AC8B6 (AU-MED-102 embryology, "the zona pellucida blocks polyspermy") rather than minted fresh -- its own definition already opens by calling the zona "the acellular glycoprotein coat around the oocyte", covering this question's fact directly.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: What the zona pellucida is
questions.question: The zona pellucida is:

options.A: A membrane that surrounds the Graafian follicle
options.B: A membrane that surrounds the ovum
options.C: The surface covering of the ovary
options.D: A clear area on the head of the sperm
options.E: The surface covering of the testis

explanations.A: Incorrect. The membrane surrounding the whole Graafian follicle is a different structure from the zona pellucida, which sits immediately around the ovum's own cell membrane, well inside the follicle.
explanations.B: Correct. The zona pellucida is the acellular glycoprotein layer that directly surrounds the ovum's plasma membrane, lying internal to the corona radiata and cumulus oophorus. It persists through fertilisation and early cleavage, only being shed as the blastocyst hatches shortly before implantation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The surface covering of the ovary is the germinal (surface) epithelium and tunica albuginea, an entirely different structure from the zona pellucida.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A clear area on the sperm head describes the acrosomal region loosely, not the zona pellucida, which belongs to the ovum, not the sperm.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The surface covering of the testis is the tunica albuginea of the testis, unrelated to the ovum's zona pellucida.

questions.learning_objective: State that the zona pellucida is the membrane that surrounds the ovum.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 31 (b/zona pellucida surrounds the ovum); stem+options read by render (p.5)

questions.subject: gyn
questions.title: True statement about ovulation
questions.question: Ovulation:

options.B: Occurs 3 weeks after the start of menstruation
options.C: Is accompanied by completion of 2nd meiotic division
options.D: Is accompanied by pain in some women
options.E: Is accompanied by a fall in the basal body temperature

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ovulation is triggered by the mid-cycle LH surge, not by progesterone, which rises only afterward, once the corpus luteum has formed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. In an idealised 28-day cycle, ovulation falls around day 14, roughly 2 weeks (not 3) after the start of menstruation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ovulation is accompanied by completion of the first meiotic division (releasing the secondary oocyte); the second meiotic division remains arrested at metaphase and completes only at fertilisation.
explanations.D: Correct. Some women experience a brief, self-limited mid-cycle pain at ovulation, known clinically as mittelschmerz. It is thought to result from follicular swelling and stretch of the ovarian surface just before and during rupture. Some cases also have a little accompanying peritoneal irritation from released follicular fluid or a small amount of blood.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Basal body temperature rises after ovulation, not falls, because of the thermogenic effect of rising progesterone from the newly formed corpus luteum -- this post-ovulatory rise is the basis of the basal-temperature method of tracking ovulation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that ovulation is sometimes accompanied by pain (mittelschmerz) as the true statement among common distractors.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 32 (d/ovulation is sometimes accompanied by pain); stem+options read by render (p.5)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Timing of the ovum's second meiotic division
questions.question: The 2nd meiotic division of the ovum occurs:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The division that occurs before ovulation is the first meiotic division, producing the secondary oocyte; the second division has not yet occurred at that point.
explanations.B: Incorrect. At ovulation the secondary oocyte is released still arrested in metaphase of the second meiotic division -- that division has not yet completed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 24 hours before ovulation is roughly when the first meiotic division is completing, not the second.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 48 hours after ovulation is beyond the secondary oocyte's short fertile lifespan (about 24 hours); if unfertilised by then it degenerates still arrested at metaphase II, never completing the second division.
explanations.E: Correct. The secondary oocyte remains arrested at metaphase of the second meiotic division from ovulation onward. This arrest is broken only by the calcium signal triggered when a sperm fuses with the oocyte membrane at fertilisation, which drives completion of the second meiotic division and extrusion of the second polar body -- the same event that converts the secondary oocyte into a mature (fertilised) ovum.

questions.learning_objective: State that the ovum's second meiotic division completes only at fertilisation.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 33 (e/2nd meiotic division occurs on fertilization); stem+options read by render (p.5)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: What the ovary discharges at ovulation
questions.question: On ovulation, the ovary discharges:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The primary oocyte has already completed its first meiotic division by ovulation, becoming a secondary oocyte, so "primary oocyte" is the wrong stage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Same stage error as option A, and the stratum granulosum is the follicle-wall lining left behind, not the layer travelling out with the oocyte.
explanations.C: Correct. Ovulation discharges the secondary oocyte still surrounded by its immediately adherent follicular cells, the corona radiata, together with the zona pellucida internal to it. The bulk of the cumulus oophorus and the rest of the follicular structures remain behind in the ruptured follicle, which goes on to become the corpus luteum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The stratum granulosum, the follicle-wall lining, is left behind in the ruptured follicle, not discharged with the oocyte; the corona radiata is the layer that travels with it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The whole mature Graafian follicle does not leave the ovary at ovulation -- only its oocyte (with the corona radiata and zona pellucida) is expelled through the ruptured follicle wall; the rest of the follicle remains in the ovary and becomes the corpus luteum.

questions.learning_objective: State that ovulation discharges the secondary oocyte together with its corona radiata.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 34 (c/ovulation discharges 2ry oocyte + corona radiata)

questions.subject: gyn
questions.title: Onset of corpus luteum regression without fertilisation
questions.question: If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum starts to regress after:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 6 days is far too soon; the corpus luteum of menstruation has a fixed functional lifespan considerably longer than this before it begins to regress.
explanations.B: Correct. In the absence of a rescuing pregnancy signal (hCG), the corpus luteum of menstruation has a fixed lifespan of about 12-14 days from ovulation before it begins to regress into the fibrous corpus albicans. Its falling progesterone (and estrogen) output as it regresses is what triggers the endometrium to shed, producing menstruation roughly 14 days after ovulation -- this near-constant luteal-phase length is why the follicular phase, not the luteal phase, is the variable part of a normal menstrual cycle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 20 days is beyond the corpus luteum of menstruation's fixed lifespan.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 21-24 days is well beyond the corpus luteum of menstruation's fixed lifespan.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 25-30 days is well beyond the corpus luteum of menstruation's fixed lifespan, closer to a full cycle length than to the luteal phase alone.

questions.learning_objective: State that the corpus luteum of menstruation begins to regress about 12-14 days after ovulation if fertilisation does not occur.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 35 (b/corpus luteum of menstruation starts to regress after 12-14 days)

questions.subject: gyn
questions.title: How long the corpus luteum of pregnancy remains active
questions.question: Corpus luteum of pregnancy remains active till:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 14 days after fertilisation is only about when implantation is completing -- far too early for hCG rescue to have run its course.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The end of implantation (roughly the end of the second week) is only the point at which the corpus luteum is first rescued by hCG, not when its active lifespan ends.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The corpus luteum of pregnancy does not remain active for the whole pregnancy; the placenta takes over progesterone production well before term.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The 3rd week is very early in the corpus luteum of pregnancy's rescued lifespan, not its endpoint.
explanations.E: Correct. Sustained by hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast, the corpus luteum of pregnancy stays active until about the 4th month of pregnancy, by which time the placenta has become fully capable of producing enough progesterone on its own. After this luteo-placental shift, the corpus luteum is no longer needed to maintain the pregnancy.

questions.learning_objective: State that the corpus luteum of pregnancy remains active until about the 4th month.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 36 (e/4th month)

questions.subject: gyn
questions.title: Sources of progesterone during pregnancy
questions.question: The sources of progesterone secreted during pregnancy include:

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own. The corpus luteum is a real source, but only for the earlier part of pregnancy -- it is not the only source across the whole pregnancy, which is what makes this option incomplete.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pituitary gland does not secrete progesterone; it drives the ovarian cycle indirectly via FSH and LH, but progesterone itself comes from the corpus luteum and, later, the placenta.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own. The placenta is a real source, but only from partway through pregnancy onward -- it is not the source for the early weeks, which is what makes this option incomplete.
explanations.D: Correct. Progesterone during pregnancy comes from two sequential sources: the corpus luteum (sustained by hCG) dominates production for roughly the first 3-4 months, after which the placenta takes over as the main source for the remainder of pregnancy. Together these two structures are the sources of progesterone across the full course of pregnancy -- the pituitary plays no direct secretory role.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "All of the above" wrongly includes the pituitary gland, which does not secrete progesterone at all.

questions.learning_objective: State that the corpus luteum and the placenta are the two sources of progesterone during pregnancy.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 37 (d/corpus luteum & placenta)

questions.subject: gyn
questions.title: Mechanism of contraceptive pills
questions.question: Contraceptive pills act by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Contraceptive pills act before fertilisation can occur; they are not spermicidal or embryocidal agents.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Contraceptive pills do not act by killing sperm; that is the mechanism of a barrier method's spermicide, not a hormonal pill.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Combined contraceptive pills contain estrogen and progestogen (progesterone-like), not androgenic, hormone activity.
explanations.D: Correct. Combined oral contraceptive pills supply exogenous estrogen and progestogen that, through negative feedback, suppress pituitary FSH and LH release. Without an adequate FSH signal, the ovarian follicles fail to mature and no dominant follicle is selected, so the LH surge that would trigger ovulation never happens -- suppressing follicle maturation is the mechanism that prevents ovulation and pregnancy.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Contraceptive pills do not stop menstrual flow; in a standard cyclical regimen, a withdrawal bleed still occurs during the pill-free (or placebo) interval.

questions.learning_objective: State that contraceptive pills act by suppressing follicle maturation.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 38 (d/contraceptive pills suppress follicle maturation)

questions.subject: gyn
questions.title: Hormonal control of the follicular phase
questions.question: The follicular phase of the ovarian cycle is under the control of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Progesterone is the dominant hormone of the luteal phase, not the follicular phase, and it is low during follicular development.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The corpus luteum has not yet formed during the follicular phase; it forms only after ovulation, from the collapsed follicle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Luteinizing hormone drives the mid-cycle surge that triggers ovulation and then luteinises the residual follicle, rather than driving the follicular growth phase itself.
explanations.D: Correct. Pituitary follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) rises early in the cycle and drives the recruitment and growth of a cohort of ovarian follicles, one of which becomes dominant, during the follicular phase. Rising estrogen from the maturing follicle then feeds back to trigger the LH surge that ends this phase at ovulation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Option D correctly names pituitary FSH as the controlling hormone, so "none of the above" is not correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that pituitary FSH controls the follicular phase of the ovarian cycle.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 39 (d/pituitary FSH)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Normal haploid chromosome number of the human
questions.question: The normal haploid chromosome number of the human is:

options.D: 23 autosomes + a male or female sex chromosome
options.E: 22 autosomes + a male or female sex chromosome

explanations.A: Incorrect. A haploid gamete carries only one sex chromosome, not two -- "2 identical sex chromosomes" describes a diploid female pattern (XX), not a haploid one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Same error as option A: two sex chromosomes, identical or not, describes a diploid cell, not a haploid gamete, which carries only one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The autosome count of 23 is wrong for a haploid cell (22 pairs of autosomes halve to 22, not 23), and two sex chromosomes again describes a diploid pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The autosome count of 23 overstates the haploid autosome number; halving the diploid 44 autosomes gives 22, not 23.
explanations.E: Correct. A haploid gamete (sperm or ovum) carries 22 autosomes plus a single sex chromosome -- either X or Y in a sperm, always X in an ovum. This is exactly half the diploid somatic-cell complement of 44 autosomes plus 2 sex chromosomes, as expected from a reduction division.

questions.learning_objective: State that the normal haploid gamete carries 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 40 (e/22 autosomes + male or female sex chromosome); stem+options read by render (p.7)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: When differentiation of the male primordial germ cells begins
questions.question: Differentiation of the primordial germ cells in the male begins at:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The 3rd month of intrauterine life is when the primordial germ cells arrive in and colonise the developing gonad -- the earlier migratory step -- not when they differentiate into the active spermatogenic series this bank tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The 9th month of intrauterine life is not a recognised milestone for male germ-cell differentiation; the testis is largely quiescent in this respect between colonisation and puberty.
explanations.C: Incorrect. At birth, the male germ cells remain undifferentiated spermatogonia; active differentiation into the spermatogenic series has not yet begun.
explanations.D: Correct. Unlike oogenesis, which begins in fetal life, active differentiation of the male germ line into functioning spermatogenesis is switched on only at puberty. This onset is driven by the maturing hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Once started, spermatogenesis then continues without interruption into old age, unlike the cyclical, arrest-and-resume pattern seen in the female.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Option D correctly names puberty, so "none of the above" is not correct.

questions.subtopic: Gametogenesis timing in male vs female
questions.learning_objective: State that active differentiation of the male germ line begins at puberty.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 41 (d/puberty); stem+options read by render (p.7)
field_notes.reuse: Overlaid onto the live Kasr concept CON-DEV-623698E111AA4B ("spermatogenesis runs continuously from puberty to old age..."), which already states this exact fact, rather than minted fresh.

questions.author_notes: "Differentiation of the primordial germ cells" is loose bank phrasing for what the rest of this bank (and the reused concept) calls gametogenesis/spermatogenesis proper; the earlier step of PGC migration and gonadal colonisation (which does occur in intrauterine life, distractor A) is a distinct, earlier event not being tested here.

questions.subject: androl
questions.title: Cells not capable of dividing to increase male germ cell numbers
questions.question: Which of the following cells are not capable of cell division & increasing the number of male germ cells?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Spermatogonia are mitotically active stem cells; some continue dividing throughout adult life, both renewing the stem population and increasing germ cell numbers.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Primary spermatocytes do divide -- the first meiotic division -- so they do contribute to increasing cell numbers, even though it is a reduction division rather than an identical-copy one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Secondary spermatocytes do divide -- the second meiotic division -- likewise increasing cell numbers.
explanations.D: Correct. The spermatid is the end-product of the second meiotic division and does not divide again; it only remodels its existing structure through spermiogenesis. It is therefore the one cell in this list incapable of any further division, and so it cannot increase the number of male germ cells.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "All of the above" wrongly includes spermatogonia and both spermatocyte stages, which do divide; only the spermatid does not.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the spermatid as the male germ cell incapable of further division.

questions.subject: androl
questions.title: Spermiogenesis facts, EXCEPT
questions.question: As regards spermiogenesis, all are true EXCEPT:

options.A: The nucleus contains half the number of chromosomes
options.C: Mitochondria form the bulk of the middle piece
options.D: The centrioles form the axial filament
options.E: Cytoplasm forms the head of the sperm

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this is a true statement, not the exception). The spermatid entering spermiogenesis is already haploid, so its nucleus carries half the diploid chromosome number, and this halved number is simply carried forward unchanged through spermiogenesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this is a true statement, not the exception). The Golgi zone does become the acrosome, its proacrosomal granules coalescing into the acrosomal vesicle that spreads over the condensing nucleus.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this is a true statement, not the exception). Mitochondria do migrate to and form the bulk of the middle piece, wrapping helically around the proximal part of the tail.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this is a true statement, not the exception). The centrioles do form the axial filament (axoneme), the microtubule core that runs the length of the sperm tail.
explanations.E: Correct -- this is the false statement, the exception. Cytoplasm does not form the sperm head; on the contrary, most of the spermatid's cytoplasm is shed as a residual body during spermiogenesis. The head is formed from the condensed nucleus (covered by the acrosomal cap), not from retained cytoplasm.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that cytoplasm does not form the sperm head -- most is shed -- as the false statement about spermiogenesis.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 43, letter only (e), no remark printed on this row; stem+options read by render (p.7)

questions.subject: gyn
questions.title: Coverings of the ovulated secondary oocyte
questions.question: When the 2ry oocyte is ovulated, it is surrounded by:

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own, and wrongly included in "all of the above". The theca interna is a vascular, steroidogenic layer of the follicle wall that stays behind in the ovary and contributes to the corpus luteum; it does not travel out with the ovulated oocyte.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own, since it names only one of the two coverings that travel with the oocyte, even though it is one of the correct pair.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own, since it names only one of the two coverings that travel with the oocyte, even though it is one of the correct pair.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "All of the above" wrongly includes the theca interna, which remains in the ovary rather than surrounding the discharged oocyte.
explanations.E: Correct. The ovulated secondary oocyte carries out two coverings with it: the zona pellucida, the acellular glycoprotein coat immediately around its membrane, and the corona radiata, the layer of adherent follicular cells external to that. The theca interna, the stratum granulosum lining the follicle wall, and the rest of the cumulus mass all remain behind in the ruptured follicle.

questions.learning_objective: State that the ovulated secondary oocyte is surrounded by the zona pellucida and corona radiata only.

questions.subject: gyn
questions.title: True statement about the secretory phase of the menstrual cycle
questions.question: During the progestational (secretory) phase of the menstrual cycle:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Follicle maturation is a follicular-phase event, driven by rising FSH before ovulation; by the secretory phase the dominant follicle has already ovulated and become the corpus luteum.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Under progesterone's influence, the endometrial glands become coiled and dilated, actively secreting glycogen-rich fluid, not constricted.
explanations.C: Correct. Progesterone from the corpus luteum drives the spiral arteries of the endometrium to elongate and coil into a markedly tortuous pattern during the secretory phase, alongside glandular coiling and secretion, preparing the endometrium to support a possible implanting blastocyst. This same coiled architecture is what allows the spiral arteries to constrict sharply if fertilisation fails, precipitating the ischaemia that triggers menstrual shedding.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Progesterone rises through most of the secretory phase, sustained by the corpus luteum, only dropping late in the phase if fertilisation does not occur and the corpus luteum regresses.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The endometrium is at its thickest, most vascular and most glandular during the secretory phase, not thin -- a thin endometrium instead describes the early proliferative phase, just after menstrual shedding.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that the spiral arteries become tortuous as the true statement about the secretory phase of the menstrual cycle.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.9 row 45 (c/arteries are tortuous); stem+options read by render (p.7)
